one_liner: Research framework that decomposes regexes into reordered sub-matches via a bandit-picked plan, layered on RE2/PCRE2/Boost/ICU.
what_it_does: BLARE speeds up repeated regex matching over large line-oriented corpora by splitting one regex into components and evaluating them in a non-left-to-right order chosen by a multi-armed-bandit policy, instead of matching the whole pattern in one pass. It is not a standalone regex engine: it wraps RE2, PCRE2, Boost.Regex, or ICU Regex and exposes free functions per backend, e.g. BlareRE2(lines, reg_string), returning a (time, match_count, other) tuple, rather than a drop-in Regex/RE2 object. Callers build one of the four blare_<engine> targets and call its function directly on a vector of input lines plus the regex string.
how_it_is_fast: The regex is split (3-way split_regex or N-way split_regex_multi) into sub-patterns, and a multi-armed-bandit policy picks which sub-pattern to evaluate first based on observed cost/selectivity, so cheap or highly discriminating fragments reject non-matching lines before the full pattern is ever run through the underlying engine. Because the same regex is reused across many lines (log/dataset scanning), the bandit amortizes its exploration cost and converges on a near-optimal evaluation order for that workload; the final per-fragment match still calls the wrapped engine (RE2/PCRE2/Boost/ICU), so BLARE is an execution-order optimizer on top of those engines, not a replacement matcher.
when_to_use: Batch, single-threaded scanning of many lines against one recurring regex (e.g. log parsing, dataset filtering) where the bandit can amortize warm-up
You already depend on RE2, PCRE2, Boost.Regex, or ICU Regex and want extra throughput without switching engines
Regexes with decomposable structure (alternations, literal anchors) that benefit from evaluating a cheap/selective piece first
Reproducing or extending the SIGMOD 2023 paper's results, using original_codebase/BLARE_CODE for exact numbers
First-match-per-line extraction workloads similar to the paper's US-Accidents / production log benchmarks
when_not_to_use: Any production dependency requiring maintenance or support: last commit 2023-11-20, 9 stars, 0 forks, no CI visible
Anywhere licensing matters: no LICENSE file, so GitHub marks it all-rights-reserved by default
Environments that can't add Abseil, Boost >=1.65.1, ICU4C, and PCRE2/jPCRE2 as build dependencies
Multi-threaded or latency-sensitive services: paper benchmarks are single-threaded only; thread safety is not documented
Anything needing the exact paper numbers from current main: README states main-branch code 'may not produce results identical to that in the BLARE paper'
Non-Linux targets: build instructions are Ubuntu/apt-based and the original experiment flags use -march=native, tying binaries to the build host's CPU

integration.dependencies: Abseil, Boost (>=1.65.1), RE2, PCRE2 10.40 via jPCRE2 (JIT), ICU4C 72, CMake (>=3.14), git-lfs for the sample dataset
integration.platforms: Linux/Ubuntu per documented build steps; macOS/Windows not documented; original experiment binaries built with -march=native are host-CPU-specific
integration.thread_safety: not documented — all reported benchmarks are single-threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: wraps RE2/PCRE2/Boost/ICU internally but exposes its own free functions (e.g. BlareRE2(lines, reg_string) -> tuple) per backend rather than each engine's native API, so callers must adopt BLARE's function signatures instead of swapping a header

gotchas: Main-branch code is under active change and the README itself warns it may not reproduce the paper's numbers; use original_codebase/BLARE_CODE for that
No LICENSE file is present (GitHub reports 'license: none'), so usage/redistribution rights are unclear by default
The bundled US-Accidents CSV requires 'git lfs pull'; a newer Kaggle CSV format breaks the hard-coded read_traffic parser and needs manual edits
Two of the three paper workloads (DB-X, System-Y) are Microsoft-internal logs and cannot be rerun outside Microsoft; only the 1.6x-vs-RE2 US-Accidents result is publicly reproducible
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick BLARE over re2jit or rejit only when the goal is specifically reproducing or studying the SIGMOD 2023 decomposition/bandit technique on RE2, PCRE2, Boost, or ICU; for a production RE2 speedup, re2jit is the safer sibling (20-30% faster on capture-group workloads, no extra Abseil/Boost/ICU/PCRE2 dependency chain) since BLARE is stale and unlicensed.
verified_claims_summary: The peer-reviewed paper (Proc. ACM Manag. Data 1(2), Art. 152, SIGMOD 2023), run single-threaded on an Azure Xeon Platinum 8370C VM with C++17 code at -O3, reports BLARE 1.6x-3.7x faster than RE2 (09-2022 build), 3.4x-7.9x faster than Boost 1.65.1, and 3.1x to over 100x faster than PCRE2 10.40/JIT, across 2 Microsoft-internal production log workloads and the public US-Accidents Kaggle dataset; only the RE2/US-Accidents comparison (~1.6x) can be independently rerun from the public repo, and the ACM DOI page returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches (paper is mirrored as BLARE.pdf in the repo).
status_note: Stale research prototype (last commit 2023-11-20, 9 stars, no LICENSE) — useful as a reference implementation of the decompose-and-reorder technique, not something to take a runtime dependency on.
